title: Why Reading Matters in Math
author: Abby Gordon
summary: Gordon recounts a 10th grade Algebra class for students who failed the Regents exam, where a two-way table problem about vitamin C stalled on vocabulary such as placebo. She argues that teachers should scaffold the context of a problem rather than strip it down to procedures, because doing so builds reading skill and background knowledge. A brief explicit teaching moment inside an inquiry-based curriculum let students access the task, and one student connected it to the placebo effect. She links this to the Pygmalion effect, claiming that simplifying everything for the neediest students signals low expectations. The move is to turn a classroom anecdote into a case against procedure-only math instruction.
points: Reading difficulties in a math problem can be addressed by scaffolding vocabulary in the moment rather than removing the context.
Making sense of the scenario taught students how experiments work and strengthened their reading, not just the table procedure.
Explicit teaching and inquiry-based curricula are not a binary, as a short definition inside an inquiry lesson showed.
Simplifying problems for the neediest students sends a message of low expectations, which the Pygmalion effect turns into self-fulfilling prophecy.
Math taught as only numbers may help students pass a narrow test while denying them learning useful in the rest of their lives.
quotes: By making sense of the scenario, they learned a bit about how experiments work, they strengthened their reading skills, and they might now have an understanding that will help them in future science classes.

After defining it for them (a moment of explicit teaching in the middle of an inquiry-based curriculum, for all those who still think there’s a binary), one young man blurted out, “Oh, like the placebo effect! I get it now!

Many of the students are reading well below grade level (some barely reading at all). So do we dumb things down for them and strip the problems of their context, hoping they’ll memorize enough procedures that they’ll pass the test? That would be doing them a terrible disservice.

We give them access to the math by providing the scaffolding they need in the moment. We adjust the lesson slightly so they have the tools they need – a vocabulary word, for instance – to tackle the problem.
More importantly, simplifying everything for our neediest students sends the message that we believe they can’t handle hard problems. And people live up (or down) to expectations.

Skipping over or simplifying the context of a problem because you think it’s too hard for your students isn’t just lowering your expectations; it’s denying them the chance to improve their reading and gain a little information that might help them become part of an educated world.

When people argue that math should be just about the numbers – and they think they’re helping their students by making it this way – I would argue that all they’re doing, maybe, is helping them pass a very particular kind of test.
